(CNN) -- Boeing is asking pilots who fly its 737 jets to pay careful attention to flight instruments after Dutch investigators said a faulty altimeter contributed to the recent crash of a 737 in the Netherlands. Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 broke into three pieces near Schiphol Airport on February 25. The 737 is the most widely flown jet in commercial aviation. More than 6,000 have been sold, according to Boeing. "Boeing reminds all operators to make sure flight crews pay close attention to all primary flight controls during critical stages of a flight," Boeing spokesman Jim Proulx told CNN on Thursday. On February 25, Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 from Istanbul to Amsterdam dropped from the sky on approach to the landing strip at Schiphol Airport, breaking into three pieces in a muddy field. Nine people died and 80 people were hurt in the accident. In a memo to pilots, Boeing says there was a malfunction in one of the plane's two altimeters, which measure the altitude above the terrain where the plane is going to land. The left altimeter was giving "erroneous" information, indicating that the plane was below 7 or 8 feet from ground level when it was actually about 2,000 feet in the air, the memo said. That caused the automatic throttles to slow the plane down. "Boeing recommends operators inform flight crews of the above investigation details and the (Dutch Safety Board) interim report when it is released. In addition, crews should be reminded to carefully monitor primary flight instruments," the memo said. The plane was on automatic pilot when it crashed, said Pieter van Vollenhoven, head of the Dutch Safety Board. The weather was misty at the time of the crash, possibly keeping the pilots from noticing their altitude, Van Vollenhoven said. Automatic pilot should not be used for landings if altimeters are malfunctioning, he said. Dutch investigators said there had been faulty meter readings on two other flights of the same jet, but the pilots were able to land. In the Amsterdam crash, the pilots did not recognize the altimeter problem until it was too late, Van Vollenhoven said. The Boeing memo notes that "the autothrottle, which uses the left radio altimeter data, transitioned to landing flare mode and retarded the throttles to the idle stop. The throttles remained at the idle stop for approximately 100 seconds during which time the airspeed decreased to approximately 40 knots below the selected approach speed." Proulx said he did not know what that speed was for that particular 737 model. The warning issued by Boeing was for many other models of 737 jets, not just the 737-800 involved in the Amsterdam crash.

# Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 Crash: Investigation Reveals Fatal Chain of Technical and Human Factors

## Summary of the Disaster

On February 25, 2009, Turkish Airlines Flight 1951, a Boeing 737-800, crashed into a field near Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport during its approach for landing. The aircraft, arriving from Istanbul, came down approximately 1.5 kilometers short of the runway. The crash killed 9 people, including all three pilots, and injured more than 80 of the 135 people on board.

## The Primary Cause: A Faulty Radio Altimeter

Investigators from the Dutch Safety Board determined that the accident was triggered by a malfunctioning **left radio altimeter**, the instrument that measures the aircraft's height above the ground.

During the approach, the left radio altimeter suddenly and erroneously registered an altitude of **-8 feet**, indicating the aircraft was essentially at or below ground level—when in reality it was still flying at approximately 1,950 feet. This false reading became the critical trigger for the subsequent chain of events.

## The Autothrottle Problem

The faulty altimeter reading was fed into the aircraft's **autothrottle system**, which automatically controls engine thrust. Because the system received data indicating the plane was near the ground and preparing to land, it responded as if the aircraft were in the final flare-and-touchdown phase.

Acting on this false information, the autothrottle:

- **Reduced engine thrust to idle (near-minimum power)**, as it would normally do just before touchdown
- Left the engines in this low-power "retard flare" mode while the aircraft was still far too high and too far from the runway

With the engines throttled back, the aircraft rapidly lost airspeed during a phase of flight when it needed sufficient power to maintain safe flight.

## The Loss of Airspeed and the Stall

As the plane continued its approach with idle thrust, its speed dropped dangerously. The aircraft slowed toward its **stall speed**—the point at which the wings can no longer generate enough lift to keep the plane airborne.

The crew was largely unaware of the deteriorating situation until it was very late. When the airspeed fell critically low, the aircraft's **stick shaker** (a stall warning device) activated, signaling an imminent stall.

## Crew Response and Final Moments

The pilots attempted to recover by advancing the throttles and adding power. However, the response came too late and the aircraft was too low to the ground to recover. The plane stalled, lost altitude rapidly, and struck the ground tail-first in a field short of the runway.

The relatively soft, muddy terrain and the absence of a post-crash fire are credited with preventing an even higher death toll.

## Contributing Factors Identified by Investigators

The Dutch Safety Board's investigation, released in 2010, highlighted several factors that turned a single instrument fault into a fatal accident:

1. **Reliance on a single altimeter:** The autothrottle system was designed to take input primarily from the left radio altimeter, creating a single point of failure.

2. **Delayed crew recognition:** The flight crew did not notice the decreasing airspeed and the autothrottle's retreat to idle thrust in time. Cockpit workload during approach and possible distraction contributed to the delayed detection.

3. **Training and monitoring:** The report noted that pilots may not have been adequately trained to recognize and respond quickly to this specific type of automation failure.

4. **Known altimeter issues:** Investigators found that radio altimeter problems had occurred on this and similar Boeing 737 aircraft previously, raising questions about whether the issue had been adequately addressed by Boeing and operators.

## Aftermath and Safety Recommendations

Following the investigation, safety authorities and Boeing reviewed procedures related to radio altimeter faults and autothrottle behavior. Recommendations emphasized:

- Improved pilot training for recognizing automation-related airspeed loss
- Better monitoring of airspeed during automated approaches
- Reviewing system designs that depend on a single sensor input

The crash of Flight 1951 became an important case study in **aviation automation dependency**, illustrating how a single faulty sensor, combined with automation that trusted that faulty data, and a crew that detected the problem too late, could combine to produce a catastrophe.

---

*This report is based on the findings of the Dutch Safety Board's official investigation into the accident.*

**AMSTERDAM** — Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 crashed into a muddy field short of Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport on Feb. 25, 2009, killing nine people and injuring more than 120, in an accident that investigators attributed to a combination of a malfunctioning radio altimeter and a delayed crew response to the developing emergency.

The Boeing 737-800, carrying 128 passengers and seven crew members from Istanbul, went down about a mile short of the runway, breaking into three sections on impact. Among the dead were all three pilots in the cockpit, including a captain, a first officer undergoing line training, and a safety pilot observing the flight.

## The Central Malfunction

According to the final report by the Dutch Safety Board, the accident's technical trigger was a fault in the aircraft's left radio altimeter, the instrument that measures the plane's height above the ground using radio signals during the critical final phases of approach and landing.

During the descent toward Schiphol, the left radio altimeter suddenly registered an erroneous reading of minus 8 feet — indicating the aircraft was below ground level — while the plane was in fact still flying at approximately 2,000 feet. Investigators were unable to determine the precise root cause of the faulty reading, though the aircraft had a documented history of radio altimeter problems on previous flights.

## Cascade to Automation Failure

The critical consequence of the erroneous altitude reading lay in how it interfaced with the aircraft's autothrottle system. The autothrottle used data from the left radio altimeter, and upon receiving the false "minus 8 feet" signal, the system concluded that the aircraft was in the landing flare — the final moments before touchdown when engine power is normally reduced to idle.

Acting on this false premise, the autothrottle retarded the engines to a minimal thrust setting. With the aircraft still well above the ground and configured for approach, the reduction in power caused the plane to lose airspeed steadily.

Compounding the danger, the flight crew was conducting the approach with the autopilot engaged and had been cleared for an instrument landing system (ILS) approach. The crew failed to notice the decaying airspeed as the aircraft slowed toward a dangerous condition.

## The Stall

As speed bled away, the aircraft approached an aerodynamic stall. The stick shaker — a warning device that vibrates the control column to alert pilots of an impending stall — activated when the airspeed dropped to approximately 110 knots.

By the time the crew recognized the emergency and attempted to apply full power to recover, the aircraft was too low and too slow. It stalled and dropped rapidly, striking the ground at high vertical velocity.

## Findings and Contributing Factors

The Dutch Safety Board's investigation identified several contributing factors beyond the initial equipment malfunction:

- **Insufficient crew monitoring:** The pilots did not adequately monitor airspeed and altitude during the automated approach, failing to detect the reduced thrust until the stall warning activated.

- **Late recovery response:** The recovery attempt came too late and, initially, the correct stall recovery procedure was not fully executed, further reducing the chances of avoiding impact.

- **Crew workload:** The presence of a first officer undergoing line training added to cockpit dynamics and workload during a busy phase of flight.

- **Known altimeter issues:** The report noted that radio altimeter faults on Boeing 737s were a recognized issue, and questioned whether operators and manufacturers had done enough to address the vulnerability of automated systems to such faulty inputs.

The investigation drew attention to the broader risk of automation dependency, in which flight crews place excessive trust in automated systems and are slower to intervene when those systems behave unexpectedly.

## Aftermath

Following the accident, aviation authorities and Boeing reviewed procedures related to radio altimeter faults and the design logic connecting altimeter data to the autothrottle. Recommendations emphasized improved crew training on monitoring during automated approaches and better handling of anomalous instrument readings.

The crash stands as a case study in aviation safety circles on the interplay between mechanical failure and human factors, illustrating how a single faulty sensor, absent timely human intervention, can escalate into catastrophe.
